Evaluation Team ii F R O N T M AT T E R Disclaimer This report presents an independent impact evaluation of the Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM) investments in Nigeria. The evaluation was commissioned by the Global Fund through the Principal Recipients — the National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA), the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme (NTBLCP) and the Lagos State Ministry of Health. The evaluation was conducted by Jhpiego (Affiliate of Johns Hopkins University) as the technical evaluation partner. The findings, interpretations, conclusions and recommendations expressed in this report are those of the evaluation team. They do not necessarily represent the official positions of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, the Government of Nigeria, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, NACA, NTBLCP, or any of the institutions that participated in the evaluation.

t: Disclaimer The report draws on data
x: Disclaimer The report draws on data collected from national, state and facility-level sources and on documentary records made available to the evaluation team. While reasonable measures were taken to verify and triangulate the information presented, the analysis reflects the data available at the time of fieldwork; investments that were ongoing at that time are identified as such, and conclusions concerning them are correspondingly qualified. All data are presented in deidentified form. Key informants are referred to by role and state, and no individual respondent can be identified from the contents of this report. iii F R O N T M AT T E R Foreword The COVID-19 pandemic represented one of the greatest tests of Nigeria's health system in recent history. It challenged institutions at every level and demanded a response that extended beyond traditional programme boundaries. What began as an urgent effort to save lives and contain transmission evolved into a broader national effort to strengthen systems, protect essential services, and improve preparedness for future public health threats.

t: The Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism
x: The Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM) provided Nigeria with an important financing window to pursue these objectives simultaneously. While supporting the immediate response to COVID-19, the investments increasingly shifted toward building resilient and sustainable systems for health. Resources initially directed to diagnostics, treatment, oxygen and infection prevention gradually expanded into strengthening laboratory networks, surveillance systems, emergency preparedness, supply chains, digital health platforms, the health workforce, and mechanisms to safeguard HIV, tuberculosis and malaria services. This report is therefore not only an evaluation of the emergency response, but also of how crisis-driven investments contributed to longer-term health system resilience. As Principal Recipient for the larger share of the C19RM portfolio, the National Agency for the Control of AIDS worked closely with the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme, federal and state institutions, Sub-Recipients, Technical Support Organisations, civil society organisations, development partners and the Country Coordinating Mechanism to implement this complex and evolving portfolio.

t: The achievements described in this report
x: The achievements described in this report are the product of this collective effort and of the commitment demonstrated by institutions and frontline workers across the country. This evaluation comes at an important moment. Nigeria is advancing the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and strengthening implementation of the National Action Plan for Health Security. Understanding which investments translated into durable capacities, which gains remain vulnerable, and what lessons should inform future investments is essential as the country moves toward greater domestic ownership and prepares for the next generation of health security challenges. I welcome the rigour and independence with which this evaluation was conducted. By combining internationally recognised evaluation criteria with a theory-based contribution analysis, the report provides a balanced assessment of what was achieved, the contextual factors that shaped implementation, and the areas where further action is required. Beyond accountability, it offers practical lessons for sustaining the capacities built through C19RM and for informing future investments under the Global Fund and other health security initiatives.

t: I wish to acknowledge the Global
x: I wish to acknowledge the Global Fund for its continued partnership and support to Nigeria, the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme for its stewardship of key components of the portfolio, the Federal Ministry of Health, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency, state governments, implementing partners, civil society organisations and all those who contributed to the implementation of these investments. I also commend the evaluation team for undertaking this work with scientific rigour and professionalism. It is my hope that this report will serve not only as a record of what was accomplished during an unprecedented period, but also as a guide for sustaining these gains and strengthening Nigeria's preparedness for future public health emergencies. The main durable contribution of the response should not be the memory of the crisis itself, but the systems strengthened through the response. t: In Nigeria, responding to the crisis
x: In Nigeria, responding to the crisis required unprecedented collaboration across institutions, programmes and partners, while underscoring the need to maintain essential services even during periods of significant disruption. As a Principal Recipient of the Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM), the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme (NTBLCP) was entrusted with key investments in Primary Health Care Revitalization, laboratory equipment, medical oxygen and respiratory care, health product supply chains — warehouse upgrades, and the continuity of tuberculosis and other essential services. Working closely with subrecipients, technical support organisations and stakeholders at national and sub-national levels, the Programme helped strengthen capacities whose value extends well beyond the immediate demands of the pandemic. These investments also supported longer-term system needs. Through the C19RM portfolio, we supported laboratory and diagnostic systems, the medical oxygen and respiratory-care ecosystem, health product warehousing and supply chain systems, and interventions designed to protect tuberculosis and other essential health services from disruption.

t: Many of these investments have become
x: Many of these investments have become enduring assets that continue to support routine service delivery and strengthen preparedness for future health threats. One of the clearest lessons from this experience is that investments in one part of the health system often generate benefits across many others. Strengthening diagnostics, oxygen infrastructure, supply chains and service continuity has reinforced capacities that support not only tuberculosis control, but also broader health security and emergency preparedness. These linked gains show the value of investing in resilient and sustainable systems and contribute to strengthening the core capacities required under the International Health Regulations. This evaluation comes at an important time as Nigeria advances the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and implements the National Action Plan for Health Security. Beyond documenting achievements, the report provides important evidence on implementation experiences, persisting gaps and the actions required to sustain and build on the gains that have been made.

It is my hope that the evidence generated through this evaluation will help guide future investments and support the continued strengthening of Nigeria's health system and preparedness for emerging public health threats. t: C19RM was designed to support the

JEE Respond-pillar trajectory: 33% (2017) to 46% (2019 midterm), with indicator-level gains by 2023. Tool editions differ; read as direction of travel. Prior to COVID-19, Nigeria’s ability to respond to a health emergency was its weakest area of readiness. On the 2017 Joint External Evaluation (JEE), the Respond pillar scored 33%, against a national average of 39%, and the core capacities an emergency response depends on sat at the bottom of the scale: there was no national emergencypreparedness plan in use, no system to send or receive medical supplies in a crisis, limited mechanisms for rapid health-worker deployment, and weak or underdeveloped health-security coordination mechanisms. By the 2019 midterm review the Respond score had risen to 46%, but important gaps remained. Nigeria therefore entered the pandemic with a system that was improving but not yet ready for a shock on this scale.

OVERALL JUDGEMENT C19RM contributed substantially, alongside government, earlier HIV and PEPFAR investment and concurrent RSSH support, to decentralising Nigeria’s molecular diagnostic capacity, modernising its laboratory information systems and establishing advanced genomic capability. The contribution is strongest and best evidenced where deployment was accompanied by activation, operational support and integration, and weakest where equipment was installed but never optimised, where reagent and maintenance financing was absent, and where delivery ran ahead of site readiness. In the first phase (2020–21), coordination that had run on ad-hoc escalation was pulled into PHEOCs as the place where surveillance signals, laboratory information and response decisions could be organised. In the third phase (2024–26), the emergency-management workforce widened to 480 responders across 24 states and the FCT, eventbased surveillance was routed into PHEOC workflows, and simulation exercises shifted the test of readiness from whether a plan existed to whether teams had practised activating, coordinating and standing down.

These are pre-and-post facility-monitoring figures from the supported facilities rather than a controlled outcome evaluation, so they are read as a contribution to service-delivery quality within QI sites, consistent with the maturity gains, and not as population-level impact. Quality Improvement is the clearest case of a capability C19RM catalysed through reprogramming rather than original design, and it illustrates the difference between financing an activity and scaling one. It was not part of the original C19RM design and had no dedicated budget line. It began under the Global Fund Service Delivery Innovation Strategic Initiative, delivered through the Resilient and Sustainable Systems for Health platform, as a pilot in five of Jigawa State’s local government areas, where Jhpiego provided technical assistance. Roughly US$2.8 million of C19RM resources, reprogrammed under the Global Fund’s flexibility to reprioritise during the response, with NACA as Principal Recipient and Jhpiego as Technical Support Organisation, then financed the scale-up: a new implementation in Ekiti and Gombe and extended coverage in Jigawa.

t: The national digital-system costs, software licences,
x: The national digital-system costs, software licences, internet and IT support, are by far the most donor-dependent stream, with about four in five assessed sites reporting these still run on donor funds or nothing (donor-dependent 79%, 95% CI 60 to 91). By contrast, the physical infrastructure has largely transitioned to domestic funding: warehouse operations are 91% domestically financed, IPC consumables 83%, and oxygen-plant running costs 76%. Commodities and buildings are being absorbed by government and hospital revenue; the recurrent costs of platforms, connectivity and IT support are not. This reframes the sustainability finding that appears in every module’s system-risk section. The risk is not a flat, portfolio-wide absence of domestic budget; it is a specific donor-dependence in the digital, data-platform and connectivity recurrent costs. The implication is a targeted one: domestic budget lines should be ring-fenced first for the recurrent software, connectivity and IT-support costs of the data and surveillance platforms, which are the streams least likely to continue after donor exit, rather than a blanket call to domesticate all recurrent costs.
